analysis.one_liner: Broadens federal protections against workplace harassment and discrimination and ends the subminimum wage for tipped workers.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or a floor vote; it sat with the Senate labor committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it easier to hold employers accountable for harassment and discrimination: it would write sexual orientation, gender identity, pregnancy, and sex-stereotype discrimination into federal civil rights law; ban contracts that force workers into private arbitration or silence them about discrimination; extend the time workers have to file claims and expand who is covered, down to one-employee businesses; and require employers with 15 or more workers to adopt anti-harassment policies and training. It also would gradually eliminate the separate, lower minimum wage for tipped workers and fund legal help for low-income workers. The Senate referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which took no action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who face harassment or discrimination — including women, LGBTQ workers, pregnant workers, and tipped employees — would gain stronger legal tools, more time to file claims, and access to lawyers through new grants. Tipped workers would eventually earn the full federal minimum wage on top of their tips.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers facing harassment, discrimination, and low tipped wages

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity, pregnancy, childbirth, and sex stereotypes an unlawful employment practice under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, and extends protections to independent contractors, interns, fellows, volunteers, and trainees.

It prohibits employers from requiring workers to sign predispute arbitration agreements or nondisclosure and nondisparagement clauses covering discrimination and harassment, and protects concerted legal action by workers.

It extends the statutes of limitations for discrimination claims, lowers the covered-employer threshold from 15 employees to 1, makes workplace harassment itself an unlawful practice with a totality-of-the-circumstances standard, and lifts caps on compensatory and punitive damages.
Employers with 15 or more employees must adopt a comprehensive nondiscrimination policy and training, with fines of up to $1,000 per violation, and $5,000 for repeated or willful noncompliance.
It grants employees the right to retain their tips and gradually raises the tipped minimum wage from $2.13 toward the full federal minimum wage, then eliminates the separate tipped wage entirely.

It establishes grant programs for preventing harassment, for legal assistance for low-income workers facing employment discrimination, and for state-based worker advocacy systems, plus a national prevalence survey on workplace harassment.

analysis.who_pays: Employers would bear compliance costs for policies and training, greater exposure to lawsuits (no damage caps, longer filing windows, broader coverage), and the end of forced arbitration for discrimination claims. Restaurants would have to pay tipped staff the full minimum wage, and employers could no longer silence workers with NDAs about discrimination.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, restaurants with tipped staff, arbitration users

drawbacks.text: Compliance carries real costs: employers with 15 or more employees would have to maintain, disseminate, and post a comprehensive nondiscrimination policy and conduct interactive training, with fines of up to $1,000 per violation and $5,000 for repeated or willful failures.

The bill removes caps on compensatory and punitive damages and lets a single incident count as harassment, which would raise litigation exposure and settlement costs for employers of every size — a cost that could fall partly on small businesses despite model materials the bill provides for employers with fewer than 15 workers.

The bill's standard allows discrimination claims to succeed when a protected characteristic is a 'motivating factor' even if other factors also motivated the decision, a shift critics of such standards argue makes employment decisions harder to defend in court.

It provides that the Religious Freedom Restoration Act cannot be used as a claim or defense against Title VII employment discrimination claims, a provision religious organizations and their advocates opposed.

Phasing out the tipped minimum wage is disputed: opponents of eliminating the tip credit argue workers in some restaurants could see tips shifted or shared, while supporters counter that a full guaranteed wage removes the pressure that leaves tipped workers dependent on customer goodwill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefits are substantial: stronger and broader anti-discrimination rights, more time to sue, access to counsel, and a path to a full minimum wage for tipped workers. The costs fall almost entirely on employers — compliance paperwork, training, and more litigation — which is the intended deterrent, though the removal of damage caps and the motivating-factor standard go beyond what some courts currently require and would raise business legal costs. The tipped-wage phase-in is gradual, softening the transition for restaurants. On balance the bill's design is coherent, but its breadth is likely why it drew no Republican support.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the Senate in April 2019 and sent to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, it never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Patty Murray (D-WA) introduced the BE HEARD in the Workplace Act on April 9, 2019, joined by 19 initial cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
All 19 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independent; no Republican cosponsored the bill.
The action history shows no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced broader harassment and discrimination liability, restaurant operators who would have had to pay tipped staff the full minimum wage, and the arbitration system that would have lost forced-arbitration agreements all benefited from the bill's inaction. Workers who needed the protections gained nothing.

industries.industry: Employers relying on mandatory arbitration and NDAs
industries.note: The bill bans predispute arbitration agreements and nondisclosure or nondisparagement clauses covering discrimination and harassment, ending the common practice of routing harassment claims into private arbitration where proceedings are confidential and outcomes favor repeat players. Workers would regain the right to sue in open court and speak about what happened to them.

The bill phases out the separate tipped minimum wage and guarantees employees the right to retain their tips, meaning restaurants would eventually pay the full federal minimum wage before tips. This directly raises labor costs for the industry and raises pay for tipped workers, many of them women vulnerable to customer-harassment dynamics.

Coverage drops from 15 employees to 1, statutes of limitations extend, damage caps disappear, a motivating-factor standard eases proof, and mandatory anti-harassment policies and training are enforced with fines. The cumulative effect is greater legal exposure and compliance costs for businesses that currently face limited consequences for workplace harassment.

industries.industry: Legal aid and worker advocacy organizations
industries.note: New grant programs would fund legal assistance for low-income workers facing employment discrimination and statewide worker advocacy systems, giving workers with valid claims a way to actually enforce them.
